Constraint Handling Rules (CHRs) is a constraint logic programming language used to model complex problems. CHRs are useful for modeling combinatorial search problems, but they can become too restrictive when there are cycles in the rule heads. A study has already examined the expressive power of CHRs with only one atom in the head, but it's a limited case, as multiple atoms in the head significantly increase the language's capabilities. We investigate the effects of having multiple head atoms on the expressive power of CHRs. We define a new concept, called input size, to measure the size of a problem. We then demonstrate that for any given input size, there's a problem that can't be expressed by CHRs that has more atoms in its head than a certain number, when compared to a version of the problem expressed using a single-atom head. We also show that for any given input size, there's a problem that can't be expressed by CHRs that has more input variables than a certain number, when compared to a version of the problem expressed using a variable count.

We have employed a new method to analyze the orientation of galaxies' spin direction in the SDSS, DES, Pantheon Survey, and the DECaLS Legacy Surveys. By combining photometric redshifts and measuring the orientation of galaxies' light, we map the spin direction of the universe's baryons. Our results show a strong agreement in the direction of the spin direction dipole across different surveys within a margin of error. We also found that this dipole has a similar direction and magnitude when measured directly from the light orientations and from the spin directions of the galaxies. The observed dipole is not due to a random alignment of galaxies with the line of sight but rather is robust and consistent across different surveys. We have also explored possible explanations for the observed dipole, including large-scale structure, intrinsic galaxy properties, and the effect of a bright radio source, but none of these can explain the observed magnitude of the dipole. Our findings suggest that a non-gravitational force could be responsible for the observed phenomenon.

We introduce Eigen-Reptile, a straightforward few-shot learning technique that builds upon the Reptile method of online learning. By updating parameters in the direction of principal components derived from a limited number of support classes, Eigen-Reptile effectively tackles two key challenges of the field: insufficient sample sizes and noisy labels. Experimental results demonstrate that Eigen-Reptile outperforms the Reptile method when training data is small and label errors are present. Furthermore, Eigen-Reptile exhibits comparable performance to more intricate and slower Reptile-based methods that employ regularization techniques.

This study introduces a novel method for detecting Alzheimer's disease (AD) from
brain atrophy images by combining a two-part classification system. The first part,
a binary decision, identifies whether the individual has AD or not, while the
second part categorizes the severity of cognitive decline using Mini-Mental State
Examination scores. Our approach utilizes a dual-branch convolutional neural network
model, which effectively integrates data from both brain atrophy images and mixed
cognitive data. Our proposed model demonstrated superior performance in predicting
AD and cognitive decline in a comprehensive evaluation using the ADNI dataset. Our
analysis suggests that the dual-branch architecture enhances the identification of
common visual patterns between the two types of data, leading to improved
cognitive decline prediction. Conversely, the data integration module enables the model
to differentiate between unique visual patterns in brain atrophy and mixed cognitive
images, resulting in improved AD classification.

This paper presents a comprehensive ethical analysis of AI-based solutions for teleworking and their impact on social and individual relationships. The authors propose a five-step ethical framework that integrates AI ethics principles into qualitative research methods, including empirical ethics, comparative analysis, and meta-analysis. This approach is applied to an existing study on COVID-19 and AI and its relevance to AI research in emerging fields is explored. The authors argue that AI ethics research has been lacking in innovation and methodology, necessitating a critical review and reevaluation. A call is made to the AI ethics community to develop a new research agenda that incorporates inter- and trans-disciplinary qualitative methods, enabling a more nuanced understanding of AI's complex ethical issues.

The study of language families as closed trios over ω-words continues, with a key focus on the interplay between their Boolean characteristics and decidability. This research specifically examines the complexity of trion languages and identifies the Borel properties within the R-TRIO and B-TRIO families, with a notable emphasis on the impact of this complexity on the decidability of each family. A significant finding reveals the B-TRIO family to be solely decidable, with its definable languages forming the only Boolean-closed, decidable full trio. This study also delves into the relationship between two subsets of the R-TRIO family, the full and the edge-trio languages, with a notable distinction lying in the Borel complexity of the full and edge-trio classes within the R-TRIO family.

A new method of estimating channels has been developed for use in OFDM systems, one that uses a deep neural network to improve predictions and, in the process, reduces the need for initial training data. The network receives input from a set of estimated pilot-induced channel values and uses these to learn various aspects of the system, including the statistical properties of the channel, spatial relationships, and frequency-domain patterns. By training the network on only a minimal amount of channel data, obtained through pilot-based estimation, it is able to make highly accurate predictions with low error rates, thus enabling high performance in nonlinear BPSK systems that rely on QAM. Furthermore, it is shown that using this network to retrain an iterative detector yields significant gains in bit error rate performance over traditional methods.

Recent discrepancies, specifically those involving $V_{ud}$ and $V_{us}$, can significantly impact our comprehension of physics extending beyond the Standard Model. The main factors contributing to these anomalies are discussed. The review delves into the status of various experiments designed to verify or refute these anomalies. The review also examines the potential connections between such new physics and other phenomena like the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, Drell-Yan high mass limits, and the existence of dark matter.

We present a novel, convolution-based network designed to efficiently compress grayscale and color images in a lossless manner. The proposed network features an innovative architecture that combines dilated kernels, transform-based compression, and prediction filters, utilizing only integer arithmetic for practical applications. The unique structure of the convolutional layers, incorporating dilated kernels and high filter lengths, necessitates the use of global activation functions, further enhancing our approach. The paper investigates various modifications to the traditional lossless archetypal network and provides a comprehensive analysis of the proposed methods. Ultimately, experimental results demonstrate the exceptional performance capabilities of the developed algorithms, significantly outperforming existing state-of-the-art solutions.

We propose a novel approach to achieve data privacy, which involves creating
transformed data views by applying a specific mechanism to raw data, ensuring
private information is isolated from shared information through this transformation.
Our method enables the creation of various data views for different entities,
each with tailored information and potentially conflicting views. The developed
mechanism can be applied to both numerical and categorical data, making it more
practical to use. Private information in the data views can be protected from an
unauthorized party as they are generated using computationally intensive functions
and distributed across multiple views to prevent an attacker from inferring a
specific piece of information from the combination of all views. Additionally, we
introduce a concept of "conflict" between data views, which occurs when multiple
views provide differing information for a specific individual. Our approach
demonstrates that it can effectively minimize such conflicts. The proposed method
is applied to both synthetic and real-world data sets, showcasing its efficacy.

We have developed a new method for identifying galaxies that have experienced mergers with active galactic nuclei (AGNs) systems. This technique utilizes the Hot Dust Observed in the Extreme: Radio mode, or H-OXE-R, index, which is calculated by dividing the luminosity of hot dust emission by the luminosity of radio activity. By applying our method to a sample of 103 nearby galaxies from the Caltech Sample and a sample of 103 nearby galaxies without an AGN from the Freeman sample, we found that H-OXE-R indices for the latter sample were consistent with those of the former, but with a higher scatter. Furthermore, we observed that H-OXE-R indices for galaxies without an AGN increased with radio luminosity, and this effect was more pronounced in galaxies with non-axial morphologies. We also found that H-OXE-R indices for galaxies without an AGN correlated with their star formation rates, and this effect was more pronounced in galaxies with non-axial morphologies. Our results suggest that H-OXE-R indices for galaxies without an AGN can be influenced by both high star formation rates and interactions with other galaxies, which is supported by the fact that H-OXE-R indices for galaxies with axial morphologies were similar to those of the Freeman sample.

Recent breakthroughs in AI have led to the development of sophisticated language models capable of producing human-like conversations, but these systems still struggle to comprehend the underlying moral principles that guide human reasoning. In an effort to bridge this gap, we've created MORALCOT, a pioneering moral reasoning prompt designed to encourage AI systems to analyze real-life scenarios and generate insights that align with established moral rules. To test the effectiveness of our approach, we've compared it to a cutting-edge AI model, and the results show that AI systems enhanced with MORALCOT are significantly better equipped to detect moral principles in everyday situations.

In 1967, Vidal claim that a valuation ring $A$ with a $p$-residue field is the long-term result of taking stable limits of principal ideal domains, or PIDs, and their intermediate rings. Although Vidal's claim is still unproven, we now show it to be true, provided the residue field of $A$ is sufficiently large, by constructing $A$ as the continuous extension of a PID. This construction relies on the development of an infinite, well-ordered tree of PIDs linked by morphisms.

The two-dimensional Dirac equation is considered across three key areas - the study of relativistic two-dimensional systems, the derivation of low-energy effective theories in quantum field theory, and the exploration of Dirac fermion systems in condensed matter physics. This discussion focuses on a specific, exactly solvable model - the two-dimensional Dirac oscillator, modified by an external potential - to illustrate key concepts and solution methods, and it demonstrates how this model can be used to describe the behavior of Dirac fermions in condense matter systems with an underlying two-dimensional structure.

In cooperative driving settings, this research focuses on the optimal control problem where a group of cooperating agents, led by a leader, navigate through a pre-defined path while maintaining a specific distance between cars. To address this challenge, we develop a Model Predictive Control (MPC) approach that utilizes a linear model, accounting for the influence of neighboring vehicles. By applying a gain-dependent Lyapunov method to the $H_\infty$ controller, we integrate the disturbance into the control design, which in turn enhances the stability during communication disruptions. To validate the effectiveness of our MPC, we conduct a comprehensive simulation, demonstrating its robustness by comparing it with a traditional Predictive Control (PC) approach that neglects disturbances.

The widespread use of social media has given rise to a culture of instant information, readily available 24/7. This ease of information access also presents the problem of credibility, as individuals quickly consume information without verifying its authenticity. Consequently, misinformation can spread rapidly through social media, influenced by factors such as the information's emotional resonance and the online environment's sentiment. This research aims to address the issue of misinformation by developing a model that integrates emotion analysis and machine learning algorithms to identify and remove emotionally appealing misinformation from Twitter posts. The proposed model utilizes a pre-trained BERT model to classify the information, while its emotion analysis component employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to recognize emotionally appealing misinformation. We evaluated this model using a dataset of misinformation labeled by human annotators, demonstrating its effectiveness in recognizing emotionally appealing misinformation.

Ensuring road safety necessitates swift and precise resource allocation by network operators in response to various emergencies. We've created the $\pi$-ROAD framework to enable effective real-time resource allocation through a collaborative operator-expert knowledge exchange. During resource allocation, operators consult with experts on potential consequences, consider expert-recommended priorities, and employ AI-driven decision support tools to optimize choices. Comprehensive data was collected from a simulated road network across 240 scenarios, revealing that $\pi$-ROAD's expert knowledge and AI guidance enhance operator decision quality, particularly reducing delays and improving choices.

This research aims to develop a real-time control system for a high-precision, 6-axis industrial robot, capable of safely and efficiently working with human operators in dynamic environments. The project's primary objectives are to enhance collaboration and optimize path planning for industrial robots, ensuring a safe and smooth interaction with human counterparts. To achieve this, the study designs a collision avoidance system using Artificial Potential Fields, a safety-centric approach that guides the robot's motion and provides a human-friendly path in crowded areas, all while maintaining optimal performance and high precision in path tracking. The designed controller not only ensures the robot's safety but also maintains its performance in path tracking tasks. The proposed APF algorithm was implemented on a UR-10b robot and demonstrated through a series of path tracking tests on a flat surface and a simulated path with obstacles. The results of the flat surface path tracking show that the robot's path length and velocity remain unaffected by the collision avoidance system, maintaining optimal performance. Meanwhile, the simulated path tracking test reveals a 20% reduction in path length, confirming the effectiveness of the human-friendly path without compromising the robot's performance.

The ongoing advancements in technology are poised to significantly impact city design, thanks to emerging breakthroughs in autonomy and machine intelligence. As a result, urban spaces will need to adapt to a shift towards increased independence and self-optimization, necessitating fresh analysis of urban layout and development. In this paper, we investigate the impact of evolving autonomy and machine intelligence on urban evolution using a game theory-based framework that combines elements of evolution, learning, and game playing. Our analysis reveals that cities will evolve into modular and diverse structures, with some areas becoming specialized and others taking on a more dynamic role. Notably, we find that a unipolar governance structure is more suitable for managing this new urban landscape.

This problem involves predicting a sequence of random elements from a universe of n elements with associated weights, and our goal is to minimize the sum of the weights of covered elements by selecting sets from a given collection with bounded capacities. In this problem, we have to make predictions without knowing the weights in advance, and we want to design an algorithm that achieves the best possible performance ratio by comparing it to the optimal solution that has access to the weights. Deep learning models for image segmentation have achieved notable advancements, 
however, they are often hindered by their excessive reliance on pixel features and 
neglect of contextual information, which can lead to inaccurate segmentation results 
especially in complex images. To address this issue, we have developed a novel Trilateral 
Attention Network (TralNet) that incorporates a hierarchical approach to integrate 
pixel, object, and scene context information. The proposed TralNet architecture 
utilizes a TralBlock, which is a highly efficient module that effectively aggregates 
contextual information across various scales. The TralNet architecture is then evaluated 
on the Cityscapes benchmark and outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods 
through a series of ablation experiments to determine the critical components 
contributing to its success. The results show that the TralNet achieves a mean IoU of 
84.5%, which is significantly better than the previous best results. Furthermore, we have 
conducted a comprehensive analysis to elucidate the contributions of the TralNet 
architecture to its performance. The code for this study is publicly available at 
https://github.com/DeepSigna/TralNet.

In superspace, the torsion constraints are invariant under supergauge transformations up to terms proportional to the inverse superspace volume. We show this in linearized supergeometry using superholoran geometry, where the torsion and curvature are reinterpreted as components of a connection whose supergauge transformations have straightforward linear representations. The connection's components are related to the superspace fields superholoran and D-flat world-volume Goldstini. The superholoran field acts as a source for both the torsion and curvature, while the Goldstini fields act as sources for the torsion but not the curvature. The supergauge transformations of the Goldstini fields up to terms proportional to the inverse supervolume are the transformations of the Goldstini fields.

The quality of training data has a significant impact on the performance of learning models. This paper examines methods to quantify the effectiveness of training data at a individual example level and builds upon previous research by incorporating uncertainty. By integrating Bayesian optimization and deep learning techniques, we develop a novel approach for evaluating data quality, where the uncertainty of training examples is used as a differentiable measure. We apply this method to a binary classification problem and demonstrate that our data quality assessment correlates with the predictive uncertainty of the model. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and promising avenues for incorporating this uncertainty into the data quality evaluation process.

In a study of a Chern insulator, we examine the interplay between the bulk edge correspondence and topological magnons. Our analysis focuses on the effects of an incommensurate magnetic field on the Hall surface and reveals the significance of the non-Abelian matrix Berry phase in maintaining quantum charge pumping. Furthermore, we propose a method to investigate the bulk-edge correspondence by utilizing thermal Hall measurements and acoustic Hall effect in the Hall surface, with acoustic magnons serving as the probe. If realized in quantum devices, the results presented here are expected to provide valuable insights into the mysterious connection between topological magnons in the bulk and the quantized spin current at the surface.

Recent language model advancements have led to significant efficiency gains, particularly with meta-learning based models like Meta-FPT8 and FastAuto. However, these models remain resource-intensive, with capacities for millions of parameters. We present METRO-LM, a novel model that leverages a dynamic, hierarchical training approach to achieve substantial improvements in efficiency and size. By dividing the training process into language model pre-training and downstream task adaptation, METRO-LM enables the use of smaller, lower-performing models as intermediaries, ultimately enabling the development of larger, more efficient models with up to 800 billion parameters. The largest METRO-LM model, with 200 billion parameters, outperforms previous models on GLUE and such as the 208B FastAuto.

We investigate the challenge of deducing a quantum network's connectivity and reconstructing the reduced density operator (RDO) of an n-qubit state given only limited information. We demonstrate that connectivity between certain locations can be determined using fewer measurements than traditional methods require, resulting in RDO states with specific properties in corresponding regions. We introduce a set of methods tailored to various network configurations and analyze their performance, revealing that for certain topologies, constant measurement counts can yield RDO states even in more complex scenarios.

This paper introduces a novel framework for creating educational materials that explain computer vision models in an accessible manner to general audiences. We propose a model-based approach that relies on a search engine to assist with the process. The paper includes the outcome of a large-scale (82,000 entries) search engine analysis on a specific topic. This information is used to compare different approaches to explaining visual representations and evaluate their effectiveness. Our findings suggest that a well-structured introduction is the most effective strategy for conveying complex information. The paper concludes with a discussion of its implications and potential future developments. An accompanying online interactive experience is also available at explaincnn.com.

We investigate how to control the behavior of complex quantum systems at the level of individual particles using optical methods that oscillate in time, and we specifically consider how these systems can exhibit ordered patterns when influenced by these oscillations. To do this, we developed a theoretical approach that builds on existing methods and can be used to simulate a wide range of quantum phenomena. We demonstrate that it's possible to control the formation of these ordered patterns using optical methods that oscillate in time, and this process involves the temporary excitation of the quantum system, followed by its return to a ground state with the desired level of order. We also show that the intensity of the optical method required for achieving a given level of order scales with the strength of the interactions between particles and the duration of the oscillations, and this can lead to reduced control over the quantum system when using very short or long oscillations.

We investigate the problem of learning optimal counterfactual policies in dynamic models with stochastic state transitions. Our approach builds upon established reinforcement learning techniques, first learning the conditional transition probabilities via a deep neural network and then estimating the optimal policy using a deep actor-critic method. However, this estimated model may contain errors, and we aim to quantify how such inaccuracies affect the optimality of the resulting policies. Our analysis shows that even minor discrepancies can significantly amplify and propagate through the policy, leading to substantial sub-optimality. To mitigate this, we propose a novel method, uncertainty-aware counterfactual planning, which generates multiple policies based on perturbed models and averages their outcomes to create a robust policy. Our method is effective even with minimal error margins and allows for high accuracy in both simulated and real-world healthcare settings.

This study presents a deep learning model that identifies sounds in a given set with greater precision by utilizing the entire dataset, as opposed to traditional methods that train models on each sound separately. The proposed approach demonstrates its effectiveness on two widely used datasets for the classification and source-localization of urban sounds. The results show that our method achieves a 1% improvement in accuracy over a conventional CNN model on the ESC-50 dataset. Furthermore, when applied to the larger US80k dataset, our method outperforms CNN models and a deep siamese neural network, while significantly reducing computational requirements. The code for our model is openly accessible on the GitHub repository, https://github.com/UsmanQidwai/DistributedDeepNet.

We explore exact two-dimensional effective descriptions for four-dimensional black holes with an AdS_4 structure, using a specific N=4 gauged supergravity model. By incorporating a suitable combination of a scalar field with a specific self-interaction mechanism, we find solutions that closely resemble those in the complete theory. These solutions encompass near-horizon versions of highly-unstable black holes as well as those with internal and external magnetic charges. We then examine the phase structure of these modelled black holes, including a range of phase transitions. Furthermore, we investigate how these modelled black holes relate to those in the complete theory, with a particular focus on their phase structure. We also extend this model to include cases with AdS_2 x S^2 and AdS_2 x H^2 geometries, which correspond to specific limits within the complete theory.

The SCAMP-5 benchmark is a recent addition to the benchmarking of SMACCUS. The goal of this project is to assess the performance of the compiler chain, including the entire sequence of Cain, Linzer, and Optimizer. Furthermore, this work compares the code created by Cain to that produced by other compilers like GHS, IBM XL, and the ICC compiler. The benchmark consists of 5 test cases, 3 of which require 32-bit and 64-bit solutions, while the remaining 2 necessitate 64-bit solutions only. The results of the benchmarking demonstrate that the code produced by Cain is significantly shorter than those of the other compilers. Furthermore, it appears that the code generated by Cain is also more efficient in terms of performance.

This study introduces a novel method for analyzing the Witten effect and a test for the spectrally spaced distribution of charged states in a quantum gravity framework. The Witten effect allows researchers to calculate the chemical potential of the thermal ensemble by examining the interaction between a thermal thermalized environment and a test probe. The proposed test further enhances existing methods by providing a more robust measurement that is less susceptible to external influences. The test has been successfully applied to the case of a scalar field in a static Schwarzschild black hole environment.

In this research, we investigate the theoretical underpinnings of regret pruning, a technique for reducing the computational resources needed to discover the Nash equilibrium in multiplayer zero-sum games by pruning regret profiles. Our study reveals that regret pruning, introduced in 2021, is a special instance of a more general framework, also referred to as regret pruning, to which we introduced a set of pruning rules. A variant of pruning rules, based on average regret, outperforms the original pruning rules in achieving Nash equilibrium. Notably, the former can be used to generalize regret pruning, while the latter can be applied to general min-max optimization problems. Our findings also demonstrate that regret-based pruning rules are optimal in certain scenarios.

This paper proposes a novel modal logic with four possible worlds and two types of modal operators, further grounded in the concept of possible scenarios or events. The logic is then applied to develop an updated understanding of Aristotle's modal proof structure, known as modal syllogistic, in light of possible scenarios. It is argued that this approach provides a more accurate and comprehensive interpretation of Aristotle's method, while also offering a general framework for formalizing any modal logic based on scenarios.

In quantum mechanics, causal relationships between events can be tested and limited only by non-zero detection efficiency, whereas in classical systems, these restrictions disappear entirely. We now show that there exists a broad category of causal relationships where efficient causality holds classically, meaning no efficiency limitations apply. This discovery broadens the scope of scenarios previously known to exhibit efficient causality only in quantum mechanics. Notably, these relationships are found to be device-independent, thus providing a deeper understanding of recent experimental results indicating that quantum mechanics may not always require non-zero detection efficiency in certain scenarios.

This paper introduces a dual-critic reinforcement learning framework for the video encoding problem. It separates the learning process into two distinct parts: one for reducing distortion and the other for controlling rate. By incorporating a cross-player training reward, the agents work together to achieve optimal performance. We implement this method in the context of the HEVC encoder, using two separate networks for each part of the encoding process. We compare the results to those from traditional RL methods that learn combined loss functions, showing improvements in rate-constrained encoding and distortion-constrained encoding respectively.

The evolution of protoplanetary disks is significantly impacted by the processes of planet formation. A key aspect of this evolution involves the transformation of a disk around a star into a planet or a planetary system. A recent study has shown that the presence of carbon-rich grains in disks can lead to a long-lasting cycle of chemical reactions. This equilibrium is disrupted when the star experiences mass loss due to a combination of magnetic reconnection and the radiation from the star. As a result, the carbon-rich grains are destroyed, releasing a large amount of carbon into the disk's atmosphere. This disruption triggers a chain reaction of chemical reactions, leading to the formation of complex hydrocarbons. This process is similar to the formation of polycyclic aromatic atributes (PAHs) in interstellar space. The resulting PAHs can then react with the disk's dust particles, leading to the formation of complex carbon structures. This process has significant implications for the formation of planets and the evolution of planetary systems.

Recent advances in machine learning have significantly improved the performance of mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers, including the selection of critical variables through cut generation. We introduce NeuralCut, a model that uses a neural network to learn the importance of variables for branching and cutting in MILP solvers. By applying NeuralCut to state-of-the-art solvers and testing it on the MIBR benchmark, we find that it significantly outperforms current methods in branch-and-cut performance and reduces the time required to find a solution in various scenarios.

A study on the intercalated chalcogenide Td-Mo1-xIrxTe2, a Weyl semimetal compound, reveals the presence of superconductivity for x = 0.375 and up to 0.5. By analyzing the temperature dependence of the resistivity, a superconducting transition was observed around 2.2 Kelvin. Additionally, a series of measurements on the same compound at varying x values found that the upper critical field Bo was 0.095 Tesla at x = 0.375 and exhibited a positive correlation with superconducting transition temperature Tc, contradicting the conventional B.T. curve. Further analysis of the compound's phase diagram suggests that the superconductivity is of a spin-singlet nature, with possible connections to the broken symmetry in Weyl semimetal compounds and superconductivity in related transition metal dichalcogenide compounds.

Information retrieval in practical settings is often hindered by a lack of relevant content, with similar documents being just as problematic when they contain unnecessary information. To retrieve relevant content effectively, we propose a novel NLP-based approach that initially extracts and then refines identical content from various sources. To achieve this, our method involves a two-stage process, with the first stage utilising a sequence-to-sequence model to identify and extract identical content from individual documents, and the second stage employing a set-to-set model to identify and refine these similarities across multiple documents. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by successfully retrieving and refining identical content in the context of software bug reports, with our results outperforming comparable methods.

A strongly coupled effective field theory for the Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) field is formulated. This theory incorporates the Coulomb interaction between charge fluctuations using a renormalized on-shell approach, which involves a physical cutoff $\mu_p$. By coupling the LHY field with a scalar bosonic field representing charge density fluctuations, a loop integral is solved in momentum space as a power series. This calculation yields a strongly coupled effective action with a renormalized coupling constant $\lambda_{\xi_c}$. The resulting phase transition in the Abelian Higgs model indicates a chiral-singlet superfluid phase transition in graphene.

We introduce a teacher-student framework designed to enhance neural network models, specifically for the task of named entity recognition. Our approach is built on a novel methodology where the teacher network utilizes pre-trained representations and employs self-training to generate labeled data, which is then utilized by the student network to learn from. This enables the student network to inherit the capabilities of more advanced models, thereby improving overall performance. Our findings indicate that this approach yields superior results, particularly when student and teacher networks share parameters. Moreover, we observed that this method enhances the generalization capabilities of the student network.

This paper presents a large dataset of social media posts and shares insights derived from it. Analyzing travel-related Facebook and Instagram content can reveal valuable trends and patterns, helping the travel industry and related businesses understand consumer preferences and behavior more effectively. By leveraging this knowledge, the industry can tailor its services to meet users' needs better, enhancing user satisfaction in the process. Furthermore, this research contributes to the development of the travel recommendation system, which can assist users in finding their ideal destinations and vacations by utilizing the collective knowledge of the community.

Microstructured materials exhibit unique properties due to their structure, but traditional methods can't be applied to analyze these materials efficiently. As a result, there's an increasing need for advanced computational tools to analyze these materials. In this research, a new approach is proposed that combines artificial neural networks and genetic algorithms to analyze microstructured materials. By training a neural network with data from virtual property calculations, it can predict the effective properties of materials. To improve the accuracy of this approach, a new method is developed to generate training data using genetic algorithms. This method allows for the discovery of effective parameters that maximize similarities in virtual material properties. By applying this approach, it was possible to analyze microstructured materials with specific porosity and observe how training parameters impact the results. Furthermore, it was found that using this approach reduces the required number of virtual material simulations to analyze microstructured materials.

This study examines zero-energy trajectories in the effective potential combination $V = V_1 + V_2$, where individual potential $V_i(s) = J_1(\gamma_i s)$ is derived from Bessel functions $J_i$, and angles $\alpha_i$ are real numbers. The zero-energy paths are correspondingly linked to high-energy circular trajectories in the isolated case $V_1 = J_1(s)$, occurring at the intersection of two spheres in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The same zero-energy trajectories are found in the combined potential $V = V_1 + V_2$. The research also shows that these trajectories separate the in- and outgoing scattering states in the scattering matrix and form a set of resonant states in the complex energy plane.

We examine a nonlinear equivalent of the Lane-Emden problem set on a four-dimensional sphere, which is characterized by the presence of a non-local, general $p$-Laplacian operator. The equation we consider takes the form $(-\Delta)^{p}\, u + \mu |u|^{q-1}\, u = u^p\, u_0$ within the context of the general $L^q$ weighted space, and we derive sharp conditions for the existence of non-trivial solutions by leveraging the principle of minimization with variable end points. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the critical $p$-Laplacian Lane-Emden problem admits multiple non-trivial solutions when $p < q$, and we also show that the modified Lane-Emden problem, characterized by the fractional operator $(-\Delta)^{p}\, u$ and a fractional source term, admits a non-trivial solution.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach to estimating trajectories in
unlabeled environments. By utilizing sequences of unassociated measurements
and prediction, we demonstrate that, without labels, it is possible to derive
basic motion characteristics and track objects. We introduce a novel filtering
algorithm that, through the use of an augmented state that includes object
velocity, can estimate the position and velocity of multiple objects without
the need for any labels. Additionally, we provide a method for estimating the
distribution of object velocity. Our proposed solution outperforms existing
methods in both simulation and real-world scenarios.

This paper presents a new stability assessment criterion, grounded in andovskaya's contribution factor, for power sideagenerators connected to the grid. The proposed criterion simplifies the determination of the area of stability (Astab) by eliminating the need for costly numerical solutions through the use of a first-order approximation. The resulting criterion is both straightforward and easy to calculate, requiring only the known system loading and the value of the contribution factor for each sideagenerator. The proposed criterion has been demonstrated to provide accurate stability region estimates even in large power systems heavy with power converter installations.

This research investigates the efficacy of employing a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) based system for developing a signature verification system. Signature verification is a complex problem, and many studies have been conducted to evaluate various approaches. However, existing literature lacks research on using a MIL framework, which is surprising, considering its widespread application in computer vision tasks. In this study, 50 signature verification datasets from 3 different identity groups, comprising 21,300 signatures, were used to train and test a MIL system. Additionally, three different feature extraction techniques were used to extract relevant information from the signature images. The results show that the MIL system outperforms traditional methods, and that the quality of the generated signature templates significantly affects its performance.

The objective of this note is to provide a geometric interpretation of the Hardy sum, specifically by equating it with the mean of an oriented geodesic's winding numbers along an arbitrary circle. Furthermore, an analogous concept is given for space, effectively substituting circles and the sphere. Additionally, a novel demonstration is provided to validate a particular finding of Hardy and Ramanujan, previously established through the use of polynomial operators.

Mobile apps frequently collect contextual data, such as user preferences or locations, but often fail to utilize this information in a meaningful way. This limitation arises because such information is typically represented as unstructured, semi-controlled variables, making it difficult to tailor experiences to suit individual users' needs. To overcome this limitation, we present an innovative approach for leveraging user context to create customized app interactions through machine learning models. This approach involves the following steps: (1) extracting contextual information from apps, such as user preferences or locations, and representing it in a structured format; (2) identifying the relationships between these contextual variables and app events, and training machine learning models to predict user behavior; (3) using these machine learning models to customize app responses to user actions. Through two case studies - one involving a social app and the other a run-tracking app - we demonstrate how this approach can be applied to enhance user experience. This approach can be used as a foundation by app developers to better utilize user context and improve their app's customization capabilities.

We introduce an efficient, real-time system for 3D human pose and shape
 estimation from both depth maps and color images. The proposed framework
 consists of two key networks: one learns to synthesize images from depth maps, and
 the other performs pose estimation from these images, with both networks refined
 through a joint optimization process. The use of image synthesis enables
 end-to-end training and enhances the generalization capabilities of the system.
 Additionally, we suggest several strategies to enhance performance, including
 techniques for handling incomplete human poses and adapting to limited training
 data. The proposed framework is the first to achieve real-time results without
 any intermediate processing steps, and it outperforms existing approaches on a
 new dataset specifically designed for evaluating system generalization.

Using the collimated instrument on board the AstroSat satellite, scientists measured the intensity of light emitted by several celestial objects. These measurements were taken in either extreme ultraviolet (EUV) or soft X-ray (SXR) ranges of the electromagnetic spectrum, and were then compared to previously recorded data. These comparisons revealed that the new measurements were highly accurate, with some being more precise than others. These findings will enable further, accurate analysis of the objects in question. These observations cover various types of celestial bodies, including stars and binary systems composed of stars and compact objects like black holes and white dwarfs.

This paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of blockchain technology,
focusing on its core principles and protocols. It delves into the characteristics
of blockchain systems, discussing the differences between permissioned and
permissionless systems, and explores notable permissioned protocols like
Hyperledger Fabric and Polkadot, alongside prominent permissionless protocols
such as Ethereum and Bitcoin. By analyzing the distinct features of various
public blockchain networks like Ethereum, Bitcoin, and Ethereum, the paper seeks
to establish a more in-depth understanding of these protocols and their
respective applications.

The improved chromomagnetic interaction model (ICM) has been found to be effective in explaining the mass spectra of various tetraquark states such as $X(3900)$, $Z_c(3900)$ and $T_{cc}(2886)$. Nevertheless, the mass spectra of the $Z_{cs}(3985)$ and $Z_{cc}(4380)$ states, which are composed of hidden heavy-flavor quarks, are not well-explained by the ICM. In an attempt to resolve this issue, researchers have introduced a new interaction term into the Hamiltonian of the tetraquark system, leading to a significant improvement in the predicted mass spectra. Specifically, the corrected mass spectra of the $Z_{cs}(3985)$ and $Z_{cc}(4380)$ states match the measured values, while the ICM also retains its effectiveness in describing the mass spectra of other tetraquark states.

In extensions of the Standard Model with multiple Higgs fields, the presence of vacuum instability due to the fundamental Higgs coupling can be mitigated by the effects of heavier scalar fields. We demonstrate that the maximum size of this vacuum instability depends on the instability scale and the Higgs mixing parameters. We then establish a relationship between this scale and the Higgs mixing parameters for specific Higgs multiple-scalar models, including the 3-2 and 45-1 models. Surprisingly, the Higgs mass can be bounded from below by the instability scale multiplied by a coefficient determined by the instability scale and the Higgs mixing parameters. We also find that the Higgs mass is limited by its tree-level mass and the stability scale in the limit where the instability scale is much larger than the Higgs mixing parameters.

In this research, we introduce a Hamilton-Jacobi equation on Carnot groups that corresponds to the $p$-Talagrand inequality. Furthermore, when the group is the Heisenberg one, a modified version of the equation is proposed, accommodating cases where test functions lack both a gradient and a second-order partial derivative. Similar to prior $p$-Talagrand research, our studies yield a variational form of the HJ equation, as well as a unique solution in the viscosity sense.

The exponentially weighted divergence (EWD) estimator is a modified version of the density power divergence (DPD) estimator, used to estimate a probability density, that incorporates a weighting mechanism for better performance and robustness. The exponentially weighted empirical L1 distance method, applied to population samples, yields the EWD estimator which has the advantage of easy computation and good performance compared to the existing density estimators like DPD, Fisher information distance (FID), and Bentley-Welch density distance (BWDD) estimators. The asymptotic convergence of the EWD estimator to the true density is demonstrated, and its asymptotic variance is derived as well. The performance of the EWD estimator is compared to the existing density estimators in terms of the Kullback-Le\'er information measure.

This research proposes a novel image segmentation algorithm that classifies pixels as either static or motion-centric without requiring any prior knowledge of the image content. It's based on the assumption that motion-centric pixels are correlated with motion-centric pixels in other images. The algorithm uses a pre-trained CNN trained with a novel loss function that maximizes the correlation between random pairs of images. The algorithm relies on a custom loss function that measures the difference between the correlations of two images and their paired pixels, and an enhanced KL divergence measure to maximize this difference. The algorithm is applied to identify pixels in a new image that move significantly between multiple frames, requiring only a pre-trained CNN that wasn't trained on the new image, and operates without needing any additional information.

In our research on the hyperbolic circle billiard, we have observed unusual patterns in the behavior of coefficients within the characteristic polynomial as the size of a $k$-periodic orbit increases. Notably, the variance of these coefficients deviates significantly from its expected value, with coefficients involving self-intersections exhibiting much higher variances. To accurately capture this higher variance, we have developed a new formula that takes into account the geometry of the orbits.

The NASA TESS mission has led to a substantial increase in the number of
periodic variables known to us, thanks to the extensive analysis of its vast
datasets. Our study focuses on a distinct subset of these variables - those
identified through the 2-minute classification technique, a method developed by
Collins et al. (2021). We have compiled a list of periodic variables from the TESS
Public Alert Package, ultimately categorizing 1,714 variables into six distinct
groups using clustering analysis. Our findings reveal a notable difference in the
proportions of eclipsing binaries and nebula variables across the six groups. 
Additionally, we discovered that the characteristics of the two categories share
some similarities, as do those of RR Lyrae and W Virginis variables. We have also
examined the spatial distribution of these variables to identify regions of
higher variable density and, in some instances, lower detection rates. Our 
research uncovered a notable gap in the Ecl Bin+NEB region, corresponding to the
TESS Enhanced Pipeline's non-linear detection algorithm.

This study focuses on a class of linear time-invariant (LTI) systems characterized by a non-negative imaginary spectrum, which can be represented as the sum of two non-negative imaginary systems. The primary goal is to identify the nearest negative imaginary system through minimization of the $H_\infty$ distance between the original and modified systems. The conditions for ensuring that the resulting nearest negative imaginary system is stable are derived. Furthermore, the induced gain of the modified system can be calculated based on the given spectral characteristics of the non-negative imaginary systems.

Continual learning aims to enhance model performance on new tasks after training on previous tasks without losing existing knowledge. This work investigates continual learning methods for improving end-to-end automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Existing research has shown that baseline methods can improve new languages with lower vocabulary sizes. However, their effectiveness on more complex tasks, such as continual learning across multiple languages, is uncertain. To address this, we conducted experiments on the LibriSpeech corpus and found that the best continual learning method can improve new tasks by 1.4% absolute in terms of word error rate (WER) compared to traditional fine-tuning. Furthermore, we observed that the best continual learning method can leverage knowledge from previous tasks with minimal loss in performance, even on more challenging conditions like knowledge distillation and multi-task training.

This paper details our approach to the 2021 Task 4 of the Cross-Lingual Natural Language Inference process. We developed a multi-lingual BERT Transformer model that leverages the entire learning rate's outcomes to tackle zero-shot CLIN, particularly for social media text with code-switching. We tested our model with a variety of settings, including different encoder languages, model languages, and model types. We observed that our model excelled in recognizing code-switched sentences within a mixed language corpus, particularly when the sentence is written in the model language's majority. Furthermore, our study highlights the benefits of incorporating additional languages in multilingual models, particularly those designed for sentiment analysis. We also found that utilizing the original dataset's English annotations can lead to improved model performance. We further investigated the impact of different model languages on our results and observed that utilizing Arabic as the model language resulted in superior performance. We successfully achieved a 0.77 performance score, ranking 5th out of 24 participating teams. We also discovered that utilizing the model language in a mixed sentence can improve performance, but this effect is minimal. We open-source our code for this task to facilitate future research.

We introduce a three-loop seesaw model that incorporates a $U(1)$ symmetry and leverages dimension-9 operators to eliminate the tree-level neutrino mass less than the seesaw scale $\Tilde T$. This model predicts the heavy particle $T$ to be less than 129 GeV and is a novel approach that may be implemented within the framework of grand unified theories. By expanding the Standard Model with the $U(1)$ gauge field and a real scalar $\chi$ with a $U(1)$ charge, we can integrate out the massive particle $T$ to generate fermion masses and neutrino masses through radiative processes. This model is consistent with existing observational data and can be effectively probed through direct detection methods.

The increasing availability of categorical data in real-world applications such as healthcare and finance has led to a rise in the use of Product-based Neural Networks (PNN) due to their ability to incorporate interactions between categorical fields. Despite their potential benefits, PNNs are often underutilized in practical settings because of a lack of understanding in the research community. This paper aims to address this gap by providing a comprehensive overview of PNNs, starting with an analysis of their architecture and demonstrating how PNNs can be viewed as an extension of the Transformer for handling categorical data. Furthermore, PNNs are shown to be equivalent to a multi-head self-attention mechanism, which enables them to model complex interactions within categorical data. We also explore the relationship between PNNs and other categorical models, as well as their generalization capabilities in the presence of noisy data. To facilitate further research, we have released an open-source Python library called PyPNN, which provides an efficient implementation of PNNs. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of PNNs through experiments on real-world datasets and applications.

This research focuses on the active beamforming problem at the access point in a system that combines intelligent reflecting surfaces and multi-antenna wireless technology, with the aim of minimizing power consumption. To tackle this issue, we employ a penalty method to create an upper limit for the power function and introduce a novel technique of power reduction for the phase shift values. Theoretical analysis confirms that the optimal phase shift values exhibit a particular structure, independent of channel state information information. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the proposed method's efficiency and the KKT dual variable's magnitude, and utilize this connection to devise an efficient algorithm for determining the optimal phase shift values. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method yields near-optimal outcomes comparable to an optimal solution obtained through linear programming, at significantly reduced computational complexity.

The branch prediction plays a significant role in performance of processors. The conventional methods of branch prediction, which utilize table lookups or simple models, are being outperformed by deep learning-based dynamic predictors. This paper focuses on a dynamic branch prediction technique that incorporates a combination of autoencoders and the Random Forest algorithm. The proposed method begins with a autoencoder-based feature extraction process, which is followed by an advanced prediction attempt by the RF predictor if the initial prediction is unsatisfactory. The proposed method is integrated with a special register and uses a simple counter to store the information, without requiring a large memory space. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can enhance prediction accuracy by up to 3% compared to competitive non-static branch prediction techniques.

This work showcases the capabilities of a deep convolutional neural network to steer a Z80-based camera, guided by a precision optical pointer, in a precise and automated manner. By leveraging this neural network's capacity for image recognition and processing, we can efficiently monitor the target through a series of small images displayed on the camera's LCD. For instance, using just a single-frame image, the system can accurately locate and track a target in a full 360-degree field of view, all without the need for complex navigation controls. Additionally, the system allows for automated camera aiming and control using a joystick, thereby eliminating the need for hand-adjusted mechanical components.

We conduct a comprehensive examination of two-player simple (SOS) and two-player stochastic (SOS) models of infinite words. Our investigation encompasses various SOS models defined by their respective order. We specifically identify new boundary laws in the SOS model that cannot be expressed normally, along with an infinite number of new normal boundary laws. Additionally, within the SOS model, we discover multiple new normal boundary laws. Furthermore, we delve into the stochastic SOS model and discover new normal boundary boundary laws. We also establish a crucial result regarding the unique characteristics of two-player automata capable of accepting words from SOS languages. This finding has significant implications for determining the equivalence of two-player automata under a non-deterministic, non-extended transition semigroup.

Theoretical models of excited-state entangled resonant energy transfer were developed, 
accounting for the influence of the environment on the coupled dynamics of donor and acceptor systems 
when stimulated by a polarized light source. By establishing a connection to the Wigner function, 
the authors have established a link between the rate of resonance energy transfer and the polarization of the environment, 
with the rate coefficient $K_{E2P}$ serving as a key indicator of this entangled phenomenon. 
This work provides a foundation for understanding the role of entanglement in resonance energy transfer and its potential in biological environments.

We assess the strong coupling constants of pseudoscalar-vector meson effective interactions from light-cone QCD sum rules. Our comparison with lattice QCD, chiral perturbation theory, and other approaches reveals that the estimations of these effective coupling constants vary significantly among different methods. The existing experimental data also fails to conform to our model's predictions. Consequently, we propose novel phenomenological models that account for the discrepancies and are consistent with experimental findings.

Recent neutrino oscillation experiments have reported anomalies that suggest a discrepancy from standard model predictions. We explore how the short-baseline approach, specifically focusing on a $3+2$ oscillation model, can reconcile the observed data within the context of the standard model with the inclusion of sterile neutrinos. Our analysis yields key predictions for various neutrino experiments, including DUNE, T2K, NOvA, T2HH, JUNO, and Hyper-Kamiokande, which will be critical in determining the accuracy of the $3+2$ oscillation model in explaining the anomalies observed in the near-term.

Linear regression techniques, particularly suitable for continuous outcomes, provide valuable insights into potential confounding variables in observational studies through implied weights. These weights can aid in study design by identifying regions where observed outcomes deviate from underlying causes, with higher weight indications of greater confounding influence. A proposed method, utilizing kernel density estimation, enables visualization of weight landscapes and facilitates associations between weight intensity and covariate values. This tool can complement traditional methods in designing observational studies and informing data collection strategies, particularly for rare outcomes where such analysis is crucial.

This paper outlines a novel control strategy for VSCs at transmission level, 
designed to suppress multicharacter oscillations by adjusting power flow 
parameters via state feedback, ensuring stable operation of interconnected grids 
with uncertain parameters. The proposed controller relies on an extended state 
observer to estimate oscillatory energy variables, and its efficacy is demonstrated 
through simulations using a nine-bus system and a 500 kV transmission network.

We have examined a model consisting of N atoms interacting with N modes of a vacuum field in a specific correlation, involving two-particle states. The atoms then decay, and the subsequent evolution of the system's state is studied. It was found that the simplest form of this model displays characteristics of non-local correlations, while a more complex form exhibits entanglement, manifesting through the presence of a Schmidt gap and non-distillable properties. Furthermore, we explored the relationship between these models and a single particle approximation, and discussed the potential for these systems to serve as quantum memories.

The existence of a lower energy minimum aside from the kink's ground state has significant implications for its stability, affecting systems such as $\phi^3$, $\phi^4$, and $\phi^6$. This understudied area of kink stability receives attention in this study, where relevant parameters are analyzed to support conclusions drawn. Research reveals that when a significant mass parameter exists between the kink and lower energy minimum, the lower energy kink is stable. Conversely, when a negligible mass parameter exists between the two, the lower energy kink is unstable. These findings hold true for multiple potential forms and boundary conditions.

High-energy hadron-resonance production and deep inelastic scattering at a collider can provide valuable information to study the internal structure of hadrons. The present research focuses on the single-spin asymmetry in the process of hadron-resonance production at a collider with the inclusion of twist-2 and twist-3 GPDs. The potential for distinguishing between different models of the twist-3 GPDs $H_{LT}^{\rm ch}$ and $E_{LT}^{\rm ch}$ is identified through the analysis of the single-spin asymmetry. The sensitivity of the analysis is further enhanced through the inclusion of an asymmetric undulator that introduces an orbital angular momentum to the incident electron beam.

The introduction of discrete noise in the training data for text classification tasks is studied, where the noise drawn from a discrete distribution alters the model's decision boundary. We develop a method to calculate a lower bound on the noise robustness using the Wasserstein distance, and utilize this bound to create a new training objective that improves noise robustness. We implement this training objective with discrete classification cross-entropy loss and a Gumbel-softmax discretization technique, and demonstrate its effectiveness on tasks involving identifying hate speech and toxic content.

The goal of polyp detection in endoscopic videos is a critical aspect of diagnosing lower gastrointestinal cancers. Deep learning models have significantly improved the performance of polyp detection, but traditional methods struggle to accurately aggregate features across the video. To address this limitation, we developed a novel video processing network called Channel-Aware Multi-Scale Video (CAMSV). CAMSV employs a channel-aware attention mechanism to enhance feature extraction across the video, resulting in more efficient feature aggregation. Our model also incorporates a multi-scale design to capture polyp objects of varying sizes and a feature enhancement module to refine features. Evaluating CAMSV on CVC-ClinicDB and ETIS-LIT datasets yielded outstanding results, achieving a high F1 score of 0.942 with minimal processing time (0.305 seconds).

A novel sequential sampling approach is developed, which dynamically adjusts 
sample sizes by spreading them over multiple rounds, increasing the total 
sample size. The method's primary advantage lies in its ability to reduce the 
risk of significant sample loss during extreme weather conditions or other 
disastrous events that may occur on collection days. The proposed sampling 
method allows for flexible control over the level of spreading, which is 
calibrated and validated using the Gini coefficient. The method's effectiveness 
is demonstrated through simulations based on two real-world datasets, showing 
that it effectively maintains statistical power across various spreading 
levels when compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the method is 
applied to a real-world dataset, which showcases its practical applications.

Type-I X-ray bursts originate from rapid neutron capture processes that occur during short-lived X-ray bursts when certain nuclei start contributing. Prior to this, these significant atomic species were thought to be bypassed, but recent findings suggest their involvement in approximately 40% of the process. However, the extent of their impact on elemental abundance variations remains unclear. To address this question, we performed an in-depth analysis of a 1.8 billion second simulation of a burst occurring on an O+Alg star. Our findings indicate that approximately 40% of the $rp$-process is produced through nuclei that were previously thought to be bypassed. Moreover, we discovered that approximately 40% of the fastest-growing elements in the process are produced through nuclei that were previously thought to be bypassed. We also discovered that these specific nuclei contribute to variations in certain isotopes, such as $^{56}$Ni, $^{57}$Ni, $^{58}$Cu, and $^{59}$Cu, resulting in the formation of the isotopes $^{58}$Cu, $^{59}$Cu, $^{60}$Zn, and $^{61}$Ga. To further investigate the role of these nuclei, we performed a detailed analysis of elemental abundance variations in the simulated ejecta. Our findings indicate that the presence of these nuclei results in variations in the abundance of certain elements, such as nickel, copper, and zinc, as well as in the formation of heavier elements, such as those

We demonstrate that the maximal dimensional components of the flat portion of abelian schemes are isomorphic to cosets of torsion groups, where the isomorphism holds naturally within a family of abelian schemes parametrized by a Noetherian scheme. This generalization builds upon the existing theorem of De Jong and Prakash which was originally developed for abelian varieties defined over algebraically closed fields.

A century ago, Cherenkov radiation discovered a new physical process and found widespread application across various fields. The discovery of ultra-high energy gamma-ray radiation has significantly expanded our understanding of galactic sources of the radiation. The Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory, specifically designed to detect such gamma-ray radiation, has provided an unprecedented view into the Northern sky. In this article, we present a selection of groundbreaking findings made by the observatory in its first few years of operation, focusing on the detection of ultra-high energy gamma-ray sources.

This research delves into nonlocal boundary conditions for diffusion models in various external environments. By altering the diffusion equation, distinct boundary conditions are formulated, resulting in distinct solutions. This paper focuses on a specific category of nonlocal boundary conditions for diffusion models, analyzing how the solution changes in response to changes in domain geometry. Utilizing a three-dimensional approach, the study demonstrates that the solution changes significantly as the domain shape evolves. Furthermore, the study presents a free boundary model, deriving the mathematical framework and employing numerical methods to solve it.

The recent gravitational wave event, GW190521, has reignited interest in compact stellar systems and black hole mergers. To create a classification system that can distinguish between these systems based on their spectral characteristics, we developed a new tool using the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) and machine learning techniques. Our training data consists of 1000 simulated SEDs from various sources, including single stars, binary stars, single black holes, binary black holes, and primordial black holes. By incorporating color-color and color-magnitude relationships, we achieved a 100% accuracy in a supervised classification system. Furthermore, we applied our tool to existing SED data and observed notable patterns in color distribution for each category. Our results suggest that g-r and r-i colors hold the most significance for identifying compact stellar systems.

Recommender Systems are crucial components in numerous applications, but fine-tuning their configurations to achieve the best possible results is a daunting task. To address this challenge, we introduce Aleria - a simulation platform for optimizing the architecture of these systems. Built using the open-source framework, Aleria mimics user behavior and user item interactions, allowing for the evaluation of various configurations. Our platform's key features include the ability to simulate different algorithms, item recommender types, and user responses to recommended content. Moreover, Aleria provides a user-friendly interface for defining different system configurations and a command-line interface for seamless testing. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates the effectiveness of the platform in generating accurate predictions, identifying optimal algorithm-performance combinations, and validating the benefits of multi-item recommendations. By leveraging simulations, developers can create more efficient, accurate, and user-friendly Recommender Systems by rigorously evaluating different configurations.

This paper presents an exact testing method for hypotheses concerning distribution parameters in cases where the mean or variance is infinite. Specifically, it provides a procedure to assess whether a given sample's mean or variance surpasses that of a reference distribution. Since conventional statistics, like sample means or variances, are not applicable, we utilize the number of partial sums exceeding a threshold, leveraging the Donsker-Dehling theorem to establish convergence in distribution. Our approach relies on a martingale difference sequence and a martingale test statistic, supported by asymptotic null and non-null distributions. A simulation study confirms the method's efficacy.

Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) have significant potential to support individuals 
with paralysis and other neurological conditions. A key component of most BCIs is 
a classifier that interprets brain activity from electroencephalogram (EEG) readings. 
Currently, most classifiers are based on a type of neural network called Convolutional 
Neural Networks (CNNs), which require a large amount of data to be effective. 

However, CNNs are limited by their need for multiple processing stages, which can 
slow down their performance. As a result, they struggle to keep up with the fast-paced 
nature of a BCI system, which requires rapid processing of data. 

To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach called the Cascade 
Convolutional Neural Network (CCNN), which enables the classifier to learn and adapt 
incrementally to the data it receives. 

By using a combination of CNNs and a learning mechanism that identifies and focuses 
on key features, CCNN can quickly process data in real-time and achieve high 
accuracy levels in a range of tasks. 

In our tests, which involved simulating various BCI scenarios, CCNN consistently 
performed better than existing models, including those based on CNNs. 

Furthermore, our results indicate that CCNN can learn and adapt effectively to 
new data streams while maintaining its accuracy over time. 

This approach has significant implications for the development of BCIs and other 
applications that require incremental learning.

The relationship between massive scalar fields at the boundary and in the bulk of an AdS$_5$ black hole with noncommutative geometry has been examined. Establishing correspondence between boundary and bulk operators, with a constraint on the noncommutative parameter $\Theta$, allows for a solution in the bulk and leads to a description of virtual black hole particles in terms of a Douglas-Kazakov phase change.

In a kidney transplantation model based on MDP dynamics, we analyze a scenario in which a patient's decision to accept or reject a transplant is influenced by its compatibility and quality of life. We incorporate these factors into the model and developed an algorithm to compute the policy and value functions. We found that accounting for incompatibility simplifies the acceptance or rejection process. We further refined the model by adding a cost to the incompatibility state, and computed the policy and value functions. We observed that this modification does not affect the policy, and our findings were validated through numerical examples where various parameters were varied.

This research introduces a novel, compact representation for Hidden Markov Models, HMM-1, based on probability expressions that eliminate the need for dynamic programming. In contrast, existing representations have to be adapted from those used in Recurrent Neural Networks, RNN, which are similar to HMMs, using their state structures. The study reveals a fundamental difference between the hidden state structures of HMMs and RNNs, implying that training an RNN to mimic an HMM is more complex than previously assumed. The research also offers a new, more efficient evaluation method for HMMs compared to the conventional approach using dynamic programming.

We establish a characterization of operators on weighted Bergman spaces that are either compact or in a Schatten class, based on their representation as composition operators followed by a multiplier operator.

Text analysis tasks often require the efficient use of compressed models that balance the size of the model, speed of computation, and accuracy. In this research, we assess the effectiveness of multiple compressed models, specifically focusing on Inception-DNNs for text classification tasks. Our findings indicate that the most suitable compressed models are those utilizing the average and max pooling methods over the spatial dimensions, as they achieve an optimal balance between model size, computational efficiency, and accuracy.

In the 2022 Snowmass Community Study, a working group on Computational Science and Advanced Computing examined the potential for high energy physics (HEP) to leverage cutting-edge computing technologies. This report focuses on key takeaways from the study that pertain to HEP, particularly highlighting areas where HEP can learn from the broader computing community. Notable insights include: (1) HEP should explore the application of machine learning in data analysis and tool development, with the potential to position the field as a pioneering user of this technology. (2) The HEP community should foster a culture of public data sharing and release of associated software tools to foster innovation and reduce duplicated efforts. The HEP community can leverage its unique computing needs to drive the advancement of computing technology. (3) The HEP community should prioritize training and develop a comprehensive training program to prepare for the expanding role of software in the field. (4) The HEP community should engage in collaborative discussions with the broader computing community and actively participate in key conferences to stay informed about technological advancements and learn from the experiences of other fields.

We start by defining generalized Howe curves and investigate their properties in detail.
Next, we demonstrate how these curves can be used to create a separate involution on the product of a generalized Mordell-Weil graph and a generalized Howe curve, which is induced by a decomposed Richelot isogeny.
This involution leads to a canonical embedding that maps the even part of a product of generalized Mordell-Weil graphs and generalized Kummer surfaces onto a subcurve of the product of the Howe curves corresponding to decomposed Richelot isogenies.
Our method enables the construction of such product curves and graphs for generalized Mordell-Weil graphs.
Our findings generalize previous research on the even part of product Kummer surfaces and provide a decomposition of the even part of product generalized Kummer surfaces.

A recent study discovered 18 newly classified magnetic hot subdwarfs through spectropolarimetric analysis. The study found 14 of these stars to be magnetically heated, which they defined as having magnetic field strengths above 0.5 MG. The measured effective temperatures ranged from 20,000 to 50,000 Kelvin, and the surface gravity was typically low. The study found that the hydrogen levels in these stars do not align with theoretical predictions. The study found no clear link between the presence of hydrogen and the strength of the magnetic field, but did note that the hydrogen levels were lower in some of the most strongly magnetized stars. The study found that the observed hydrogen levels were more closely aligned with theoretical expectations for a specific type of star that has lost its helium, known as a DAV star. The study suggested that the observed hydrogen levels could be the result of a combination of the star's magnetic field and the radiation it emits, which could cause it to lose mass at a faster rate than a typical star. The study found that the observed hydrogen levels were lower than what was previously observed in non-magnetic hot subdwarfs, and that the hydrogen levels were lower in general than what was previously observed in similar studies. The study found that the presence of a magnetic field may have caused the hydrogen in these stars to be lost more quickly, which could explain the observed decrease in the hydrogen levels.
