In multi-threaded symbolic execution, dynamic work distribution among threads is 
achieved through a shared queue system. However, this approach often leads to sequential 
dependency issues that limit the range of available work management techniques.
We propose an innovative approach, known as test-depth partitioning, that enhances 
parallelism and introduces a new dimension of flexibility in the search strategies 
and thread synchronization methods employed. This technique divides the test depths into 
asynchronous bins and assigns each thread a dedicated depth range, allowing it to 
execute concurrent operations without conflicts. This novel concept is integrated into 
KLEE and yields superior performance, and preliminary results indicate that test-depth 
partitioning can accommodate a broader class of search strategies and synchronization 
techniques.

Our research involves studying the magnetic properties of iron oxide nanoparticles when subjected to short pulses of magnetic field orientation that can vary in length, intensity, and direction. By analyzing how these nanoparticles lose magnetization over time, we were able to determine the rate at which they lose magnetization and determine the exact length of their anisotropy axis. We discovered that when the magnetic field pulses are strong enough, the nanoparticles behave in a predictable manner, but at lower pulse intensities, their complex responses allow us to determine the exact length of their anisotropy axis. We also found that the length of the pulse and the direction of the pulse are crucial factors in determining the behavior of the nanoparticles. Furthermore, we observed that the length of the anisotropy axis is directly related to the angle between the direction of the pulse and the anisotropy axis.

Federated learning is a rapidly evolving area of research, which enables the training of machine learning models on decentralized data with minimal central involvement. However, the absence of a central server in certain environments poses significant challenges when attempting to balance model accuracy and local computational constraints. One potential solution involves the federated learning of a linear model via an optimization method known as Online Push-Sum, which balances the trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. However, the theoretical underpinnings of this approach have yet to be fully explored. This paper seeks to address this knowledge gap by examining the Online Push-Sum method in more detail, focusing specifically on its implications for the performance of machine learning models in scenarios where data is skewed.

Predicting dialog acts is a crucial step in understanding conversational behavior.
Current research focuses on identifying turns within a conversation, but the context
of the conversation and the context of previous messages is often overlooked.
We developed a two-stage neural model to address this issue and improve dialog act
prediction, starting with a classification stage to determine the most relevant
previous contexts and continuing with a recurrent model to predict the current
dialog act. Our model outperformed the baseline by achieving notable gains in F1
scores across all three stages, with the greatest improvements seen in the last three
stages. Additionally, the use of short texts before the current conversation yielded
substantial enhancements in F1 scores, with the greatest increases observed in the
last two stages.

We've developed a comprehensive model for a telecentric etalon-based instrument, one that is effective at both visual and astronomical applications. Our model draws on the work of Bond (1983) and Herkenhoff (1993), combining these concepts into a single, unified framework that spans both visual and vacuum-domain scenarios. Our model enables us to examine the performance of telecentric etalons against collimated instruments, particularly in terms of their resolution, which is influenced by the Ewald sphere. When used in conjunction with an optical telescope and CCD imaging, our model reveals the Ewald sphere's effect, demonstrating that instruments with similar F-number performance can have significantly enhanced capabilities. Notably, this model highlights the superiority of telecentric etalon-based instruments, which can achieve 50-100% improved resolution, particularly in situations involving high-order spectra.

In this research, we investigate the labeling of maps under the toroidal map coloring model. We explore how many copies of specific points, denoted as $N_p$, are needed to achieve a particular labeling. We found that if a given set of points, denoted as $p$, consists of $n$ points, then it requires $2n-1$ copies of these points to allow a matching consisting solely of a single edge. We also identified specific cases where the number of necessary point copies is reduced to $n-1$. Furthermore, we found that if a matching of the map consists of $k$ edges, $N_p$ will be less than or equal to $2k-1$ copies of a set of $k$ edges.

This paper outlines a codelet-based program execution model, called CM3, which enables efficient execution of data-parallel applications on chiplet-based systems. The CM3 model represents a codelet as a directed graph comprising nodes and edges that facilitate communication and computation. The model's underlying graph framework enables CM3 codelets to be executed on a variety of chiplet architectures. The CM3 execution model also supports the execution of CM3 codelets on chiplet platforms. The paper further provides a mapping of CM3 codelets to physical chiplet resources and a scheduling framework for CM3 codelets on chiplet platforms. The CM3 model's effectiveness is demonstrated through the development of two example CM3 codelets, each representing a different application scenario. The paper also presents preliminary results of CM3 execution on a real-world chiplet platform.

A novel presmoothing technique is developed to enhance the accuracy of maximum likelihood estimators in diverse exponential family models, including those commonly used for continuous and time-to-event data. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through the reduction of residual variance in subsequent empirical risk estimators. The presmoothing process is shown to yield a more reliable maximum likelihood estimator, enabling faster convergence in the empirical risk estimator. Key properties of the presmoothing estimator are established, along with its asymptotic properties. Notably, it maintains the same rate of convergence as the maximum likelihood estimator, while offering a more robust starting point for subsequent estimators. The presmoothing technique is further supported by its empirical performance, as illustrated through several real-world and simulated examples.

The nonlocal metric dimension of a graph G is defined as the minimum number 
of nodes whose distance information is sufficient to determine every vertex's 
nearest neighbor set. This concept differs from distance vector dimension, 
where nodes are chosen based on their distances to other vertices. Optimal 
solutions for the nonlocal metric dimension problem have been found for a range 
of graph types, including those based on cycles, tournaments, and specific 
graph products. Additionally, graphs with nonlocal metric dimensions of 1 or 
n(G) - 2 have been characterized, while the dimension of complete bipartite 
graphs and nonlocal connectivity have been investigated. Properties of the 
nonlocal metric dimension have been explored through one-point and two-point 
distance vectors.

This paper presents FLUPP, a versatile side-channel attack framework capable of exploiting internal weaknesses in various types of neural networks. FLUPP employs power trace measurements to be launched and can be tailored to identify specific characteristics of multiple classes of classifiers, encompassing DNNs, CNNs, RNNs, and LSTMs. FLUPP operates by leveraging a classifier trained on power traces of an adversary to serve as a proxy for the intended classifier, thus mitigating the need for prior knowledge of the targeted model and its architecture. FLUPP has been successfully demonstrated on multiple datasets using RNNs and LSTMs, yielding impressive results that surpass state-of-the-art approaches.

To efficiently shorten polarization kernels, we propose a two-step iterative method that utilizes the Neumann expansion and the Hilbert-Schmidt criterion. This approach is grounded in the fact that the polarization kernel's decay rate is crucially dependent on the eigenvalues of its associated operator. Therefore, we focus on developing tight bounds for the partial distances and create a new method to iteratively refine these bounds, ultimately enabling the derivation of more precise estimates. This process is simplified to a series of convex optimization problems, the solutions of which yield improved bounds for the partial distances. Consequently, we can develop more accurate lower and upper bounds for the decay rate of the polarization kernel, enabling the shortening process to be efficiently and effectively conducted.

We demonstrate the capability of synthetic datasets in enhancing self-supervised denoising in real-world seismic data analysis. The process begins with training a convolutional neural network using a synthetic dataset with known ground truth, followed by fine-tuning it on actual data without labels. This approach yields improved results compared to direct self-supervised training on real-world data alone, with additional enhancements when incorporating multiple synthetic datasets. Furthermore, incorporating a synthetic data augmentation policy during self-supervised training on real-world data leads to enhanced fine-tuning outcomes.

In this theoretical study, we investigate the real photon emission process in lepton-proton scattering within the Standard Model at low energy and low momentum transfer. Real photon emission allows for the potential subleading contribution to the measured lepton asymmetry. Our calculations take into account the most up-to-date lepton magnetic dipole moments and resolve discrepancies with existing QED predictions. We have also developed a new approach to reduce the complexity of radiative one-loop diagrams in our numerical analysis.

A three-dimensional Mott insulator with a large hopping parameter in one direction can be characterized by a specific spectrum of spin-polaronic excitations. Theoretical calculations demonstrate how these excitations affect the band structure of such a material, revealing a distinct relationship between the spectrum and the material's properties. The presence of a large amount of momentum space occupied by these excitations, particularly at low energies, leads to a specific type of correlation between the spin and charge of the material, with implications for a variety of phenomena, including superconductivity. The presence of a specific type of excitation at a particular wavevector is found to be crucial for a variety of these phenomena, and numerical calculations for a specific material show that it is in agreement with the theoretical predictions.

We've developed a novel estimation method for continuous interventions, which builds upon the empirical vector machine. This method ensures that its outcomes remain resilient to variations in the data set. A corresponding statistical test has been created to determine whether a specific intervention would likely yield a positive effect. By leveraging the high-dimensional characteristics of the data, this test achieves higher statistical power. The methods and tests are applicable to both experimental data and observational data with a single continuous treatment variable. The efficacy of the approaches is demonstrated through both simulated data and a real-world study, specifically analyzing the effect of raising student achievement on student graduation rates.

A concentrated effort to analyze and synthesize existing research on starshades 
facilitates future scientific endeavors and provides valuable insights into the 
efficacy of current approaches. Recent research utilizing the method of starshades 
enhances our understanding of exoplanets, and the co-location of similar studies 
boosts the scientific significance of upcoming starshade missions. A collection of 
research findings published in prior conferences and journals is summarized here.

The recent release of the Robust Suicidal Activated Lexicon (ROBIL) represents the first publicly available resource for identifying suicidal language in Hindi. Previous resources, such as the Hindi Suicidal Lexicon (HSL) from the Robin dataset and Suicidal Intent Lexicon (SIL), all derived from online sources, have been found to have limitations in identifying suicidal content. ROBIL overcomes these limitations by utilizing the combination of natural language processing tools and advanced n-gram techniques, along with the incorporation of a manual annotation process, to create a more accurate dataset. ROBIL consists of 1,500 samples, of which 750 are non-suicidal and 750 are suicidal, annotated at character level. The dataset was found to have a high inter-annotator agreement and provided more nuanced results in identifying suicidal content in comparison to other datasets. The paper also presents two baseline models for detecting suicidal content in Hindi, highlighting the potential of the ROBIL dataset in improving the performance of BERT models for this task.

A supersymmetric extension of the Schrödinger framework has been developed, and its key characteristics are explored. This framework yields constraints on the super-Schwarzians and their invariant properties. A superanalogon action is derived from the super-Schwarzian equation, and its invariance is demonstrated, leading to a novel action for three superanalogons.

This research explores the concept of new periodic cycles emerging from the interaction of two distinct rational dynamical systems. By analyzing the collaborative behavior of these systems, we identify and develop a method for constructing novel periodic cycles in the context of difference equations and circulant matrices. The practical implications of our research are far-reaching, with applications in the fields of physics, combinatorics, number theory, and biology. Furthermore, our work also reveals the existence of threshold values beyond which the systems begin to display increased complexity.

We develop a family of electrically charged, four-dimensional AdS black holes that are based on Einstein's theory combined with a specific self-interacting nonlinear electrodynamics model. This particular model of non-linear electrodynamics was specifically chosen as it allows for a straightforward analysis of electric charges without introducing any additional physical parameters. By examining the thermodynamic properties of these black holes, we determine their phase structure and behavior, taking into account the effects of both charge and entropy parameters. Furthermore, we investigate the phase behavior of these thermodynamic systems, in which the pressure is held constant, by using the Grand Canonical Ensemble. Our analysis also includes a phase transition that occurs between small and large black holes, as well as a phase transition that involves the formation of a thermally charged phase.

To solve Sidon's problem, we focus on finding infinite Sidon sets for a linear form f(x) with coefficients a_1 through a_k, where the exponents are distinct and not just relatively prime. We show that an infinite Sidon set exists for some forms if and only if the forms' rank is less than or equal to the square root of n over 12, minus 1, plus one, minus the epsilon of any small positive value. For any given form rank, there are only finitely many possible Sidon sets, and their cardinality can be upper bounded by the exponential of the constant times the form's rank.

A theoretical analysis of magnetic susceptibility is carried out for two types of non-Abelian geometric phase generators in an open system under a transverse magnetic field. A connection is established between the susceptibility and the geometric phase of dynamic systems that undergo quantum phase transitions, which can be measured by observing the changes in electron spin state occupancy in a single spin system. Furthermore, in multi-component systems, susceptibility is found to be related to the variance of dynamic populations, and in such cases, susceptibility can be expressed in terms of geometric phase. Experimental verification of susceptibility in multiple spin systems is made possible by measuring changes in the occupation of Zeeman sublevels.

This work explores the role of critical fluctuations in ferromagnetic systems that undergo a sudden cooling process from high temperatures to their critical point. A semi-analytical solution developed here for the Ising model provides the non-equilibrium magnetization profile after cooling. These findings are compared to existing Monte Carlo simulations and confirm the accuracy of the derived expressions. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that the non-equilibrium magnetization can be used to estimate the system's temperature, a key parameter in critical phenomena. These critical fluctuations are also examined in the context of the 3D Ising model and good agreement is found with Monte Carlo simulations once the temperature is accounted for.

The effect of quasiperiodicity in quasiperiodic systems is characterized across different scales of length and time. For bound states within quasiperiodic lattices, quasiperiodicity is a key factor in the transition from localization. The quasiperiodic Heisenberg model is a significant model in understanding the phenomenon of quasiperiodicity. We investigate the quasiperiodic Heisenberg model at half-filling using a variational approach to analyze the quasiperiodic ground state. The results show that the quasiperiodic Heisenberg model exhibits quasiperiodicity and a non-trivial phase diagram. The model's ground state properties are significantly influenced by both the magnetic field and the spin anisotropy.

Task-oriented dialogue systems in multiple languages are typically trained using hand-labeled data, but this process is time-consuming, expensive, and may be difficult to scale to various languages. This paper explores the effectiveness of using automated data generation methods to train dialogue systems in multiple languages. We investigate how a shared neural architecture in different languages can produce informative data and contribute to the development of cross-lingual dialogue systems. We also examine the impact of shared vs. language-specific embeddings on the quality of system performance, and our findings suggest that a shared embedding can facilitate more accurate dialogue modeling across languages.

RNA-seq time series data from deep sequencing technology can be used to investigate how gene expression levels change over time. We propose a new Bayesian method called DESeqS2f, which builds on the DESeq2 package, to analyze RNA-seq time series data and determine how genes are differently expressed. This method utilizes Gaussian processes to model the changing expression levels over time and provides posterior credible intervals to identify significant differential expression and expression at specific times. The posterior predictive checks and model validation tests are also included in this method. We propose a new Bayesian equivalent of the Benjamini-Hochberg correction for controlling false discovery rates, which adjusts for multiple testing. Our simulations show that DESeqS2f performs well in recovering true positives and has good type I error control, even with complex time-course data. We applied this method to a melanoma data set and identified genes that show a different expression level at certain time points, which may be useful for understanding the changing expression levels over time.

To protect data privacy in various applications and meet data protection regulations, companies must implement technical measures that engineers can design and legal experts review. Unfortunately, interactions between engineers and legal experts often lack clear, well-structured input and output, leading to misunderstandings and errors that can result in non-compliant data protection policies and increased legal risks. In response, we developed a new method called ICS Map, which creates a visual mapping between technical and legal measures. Through a series of interviews and workshops, we identified key challenges in communication between engineers and legal experts, which include a lack of well-defined input and output, as well as unclear roles and responsibilities. The application of ICS Map has been shown to overcome these challenges and improve communication. The development of ICS Map represents a significant step towards bridging the technical and legal gaps in protecting data.

We develop a novel method within the Color Glass Condensate framework to analyze even-distributed azimuthal angle correlations in small particle systems. This method effectively describes the correlations in an electron-positron pair emitted through the process of Bhabha scattering. We compare the resulting correlations with those predicted by a quantum mechanics approach and find significant agreement. We also demonstrate that the initial state correlations in Bhabha scattering can be used to understand correlations in a specific type of heavy ion collision, specifically the azimuthal angle correlations in a specific type of particle system.

The production of specific light nuclei, including a deuteron and helium isotopes, in high-energy proton collisions, is studied using the AMPT model under varying conditions. This includes modifying the model to include different sources of particle formation through the Monte Carlo coalescence model, as well as adjusting the prehadron and posthadron model parameters. The impact of these changes on the production of light nuclei is examined. Furthermore, theoretical calculations using coalescence parameters from proton-lead collisions, performed by the ALICE experiment, are compared to the simulated AMPT results to assess their predictive power. The findings suggest that incorporating coalescence sources effectively describes the production of light nuclei, while adjustments to the model parameters improve the accuracy of calculations for the helium isotope spectra.

The atmospheric compositions of rocky exoplanets, especially those within the habitable zone, will greatly vary based on their formation and evolution characteristics. Understanding these variations is crucial for accurately interpreting the atmospheric properties of future directly imaged planets and for determining the habitability potential of any discovered world. We have developed a detailed model that simulates the development of a rocky planet's atmosphere, taking into account factors like the composition of its protoplanetary disk, the presence of gas giants, and the impact of volatile release from the planet's interior. The model incorporates a new method for estimating the amount of volatiles delivered to the planet's surface over time, based on the size of its parent body. We applied this model to a set of idealized protoplanetary disk scenarios, each with distinct characteristics, to explore the range of possible atmospheric compositions and their associated uncertainties. The results show that multiple factors contribute to the expected diversity of atmospheric compositions on rocky exoplanets, especially those in the habitable zone, leading to a wide array of possible compositions. The model also suggests that certain conditions can lead to the presence of surface liquid water on those planets within the habitable zone, but the likelihood of this occurrence is low.

The study of automorphism groups and spectral analysis of finite groups has been a significant area of research, particularly in relation to circulant graphs. This note focuses on analyzing the dispersability of circulant graphs with unique jump lengths not exceeding three and derives key findings regarding their distinctness, uniqueness, and Riemann-like conjectures. Furthermore, it investigates the dispersability of their direct products with other finite groups.

In the context of nested Cahn-Hilliard equations, a Neumann type algorithm is analyzed using adaptive time-stepping based on the PDE solution's inception depth. This analysis leads to the derivation of convergence rates, with the rate of convergence being influenced by the inception depth. To facilitate the application of the Neumann algorithm to three-dimensional problems, a space adaptive strategy is developed, combining space and time adaptive methods. Numerical results validate the derived convergence rates and the effectiveness of the proposed space-time adaptive strategy.

The cosmic friction term in the mode equation for curvature perturbations has been found to have a substantial impact in single-field inflationary models, significantly enhancing boost effects when the wave number $k$ approaches the effective Hubble radius $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$. This model enhancement is crucially dependent on the cosmic friction term in the mode equation. The influence of the cosmic friction term on the cosmological perturbation spectrum is significant, particularly around the decoupling scale $k_\Lambda$, which is close to $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$. This effect causes the spectrum to exhibit a distinctive shape, characterized by a double-scale feature in the perturbation spectrum. The double-scale feature is a result of the boost effect caused by the cosmic friction term, which is most pronounced in the $H_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $k_\Lambda$ regimes. The influence of the cosmic friction term on the cosmological perturbation spectrum is significant, which can be seen in the power-law index $\alpha$ at a specific scale $k_a$. The effect is that the power-law index $\alpha$ is a function of the wave number $k$, which can be seen in the power-law index $\alpha$ at a specific scale $k_a$. The influence of the cosmic friction term on the power-law index $\alpha$ is significant, which can be seen in the power-law index $\alpha$ at a specific scale $k_a$.

We examine the benefits of airlines using limited-time, reduced-price offers to draw in more customers and to reduce the impact of losing sales from higher regular fares. Our research focuses on pricing and revenue strategies for airlines offering limited-time, restricted-price deals that are completely redeemable. We find that such deals should be sold in two stages, first determining the total number of available tickets and then setting individual ticket caps. Our model is based on a scenario where customers choose either to buy a ticket or not, and they consider the potential for buying a ticket in one flight to influence the decision to buy a ticket in another. We discovered that offering limited-time, restricted-price deals generates revenue for the airline and increases overall demand, and we analyzed how different factors like the number of available flights, the number of customers interested in purchasing tickets, and the price of the deals influence the airline's revenue.

The analysis of survival data is crucial in numerous fields, including medicine and agriculture.
The casebase package offers an innovative approach to analyzing this type of data by combining the strengths of Bayesian inference and the casebase algorithm.
This combination enables the accurate estimation of parameters and the calculation of probabilities related to survival times.
Building on the casebase package, a new method, known as the casebase survival package, aims to facilitate survival data analysis with a greater emphasis on interpretability.
This package provides several enhancements to its predecessor, including improved estimation methods, a wider range of graphical tools, and new features for Bayesian inference.
This article serves as a comprehensive guide to the casebase survival package, which includes detailed explanations of its underlying concepts, a discussion of its key functionalities, and several examples of its application in real-world scenarios.

A novel semi-numerical approach is developed to compute the differential decay rate of an electron in a vacuum from a point-like $e^+$ annihilation to $e^-$ anti-$\nu_\mu$ bar, focusing on the highest order in the electromagnetic coupling constant. This method enhances the accuracy of the result by reducing the dependence on numerical methods compared to the Breit-Wigner approximation, while requiring minimal computational resources. The approach is applicable to other particle decays and has the potential to be adapted for simulations in the Large Hadron electron Collider.

The performance of traditional distributed POSIX systems is significantly impacted by the file metadata, causing them to become slow as files accumulate.  Object storage systems, in contrast, have become popular for large-scale metadata-intensive applications, but they often lack critical features such as POSIX.  Today, many cloud services lack a native distributed file system, instead offering the option to create it from scratch.  This research presents ZFSyn, a structured file system designed for cloud environments with low overhead, efficient file operations, and support for the full POSIX specification.  ZFSyn leverages cloud capabilities, is highly fault-tolerant, and incorporates multiple replication strategies to ensure reliability.  Tests have shown ZFSyn to be an extremely scalable solution, capable of handling a vast number of files efficiently with both local and distributed file systems.

As electric vehicles (EVs) gain popularity, charging infrastructure must be developed to support them. Parking lots with limited Level 2 AC charging stations are being considered as a viable option to address the increasing demand for charging facilities. However, these resources are insufficient to meet the needs of all drivers, resulting in an allocation problem. This paper proposes an online pricing mechanism that encourages EV owners to arrive at parking lots and charge their vehicles during off-peak hours by taking into consideration their travel plans and charging needs. The design of this mechanism is based on a complex game theory framework and involves a two-part approach: first, a parking lot owner can offer a dynamic pricing strategy to potential users and then these users make informed decisions whether to use the charging resource or not. The analysis shows that this pricing strategy has a unique sub-game equilibrium, which cannot be surpassed. The results of the simulation also demonstrate that this pricing strategy leads to an efficient allocation of charging resources, with significant cost savings for both users and parking lots compared to a first-come, first-served allocation process.

We suggest a method for creating different types of Hermitian Low-Density Parity Check codes, and explore the properties of the resulting codes, particularly their weight distribution and algebraic properties. Additionally, we propose a method for creating new Hermitian quasi-twisted codes from existing codes, and examine the characteristics of the new codes, including their weight distribution and quasi-metric properties.

Building upon our previous work in arXiv:2110.00178, we extend our analysis to determine the integrals necessary for computing black-hole scattering in Einstein gravity, now combined with a single scalar field. Using a black-hole effective theory, we derive the corresponding integrals up to the fourth order, which includes expressions for the double copy and three copies. Notably, the required integrals were previously known up to the third order from Black Hole Perturbation Theory. Our study also uncovers the underlying differential equation for the integrals and provides insights into their behavior, including their asymptotic properties, which are crucial for accurately evaluating the integrals through a Watson-like expansion.

Site selection for solar and wind power plants often relies on data that can cause overestimation of future costs, particularly when land acquisition and compensation are involved. A study models the full lifespan of 10 different wind and solar projects to quantify the previously unaccounted land use costs associated with these sites. The research reveals that the risk of site occupation exceeds initial estimates by up to 15% for solar and by up to 25% for wind projects. As a result, the site risk associated with solar and wind sites tends to skew towards more expensive locations, leading to increased costs and project expenses. The study finds that acknowledging these previously unaccounted costs results in cleaner electricity goals being achieved at a significantly higher cost, estimated at 24-52%, compared to initial estimates, suggesting that the site risk associated with solar and wind sites tends to skew towards more expensive locations, leading to increased costs and project expenses.

Cluster-randomized trials are a common study design used in epidemiology, where groups rather than individuals are assigned treatments and analyzed to measure its effectiveness. The primary objective of such trials is to determine the direct impact of a vaccine in a two-time period framework. Unfortunately, this effect cannot be directly calculated from cluster-randomized trials due to the contamination issue that arises when individuals within clusters interact with one another. The traditional approach to address this issue involves using a logistic mixed-effects model in a two-time period framework. The model's parameters are then estimated using a likelihood-based estimator, which can be challenging, especially when dealing with larger clusters and smaller sample sizes. The issue arises due to the lack of independence among the likelihood contributions from each cluster. The traditional approach often relies on a simplifying assumption that the within-cluster likelihood contributions are independent, which can be conservative in nature. Our proposed alternative is a moment-based estimator that is more reliable and efficient in a wide range of cluster sizes and sample sizes. The performance of the estimators is compared through simulations, and the findings are further supported by real-world data from a cluster-randomized trial conducted in South Africa, which assessed the efficacy of the Hepatitis B vaccine.

This paper focuses on deriving expressions and constructing upper bounds for the multiplicative degree-$K$ Kirchhoff index in specific molecular networks, utilizing graphs with $N$ nodes and $N-1$ edges. Upper bounds are formulated by linking the $r$-walk counts of these graphs to their corresponding adjacency matrix eigenvalues, enabling the establishment of more precise approximations for the Kirchhoff index. The methodology is applied to determine bounds for the multiplicative degree-$K$ H\"{ollerian information index in $s$-cyclic networks, extending to various network structures, including $s$-regular graphs and $r$-directed networks.

We investigate contextual linear bandits where agents learn from a class of linear models influenced by an underlying environment. The environment's characteristics are measured by its context distribution, which defines the probability of generating specific contexts. Although the environment's characteristics affect the agents' communication requirements, they do so implicitly. To address this issue, we introduce a new contextual linear bandit scenario called the contextual CLB with knowledge. In this setting, the environment not only influences the reward functions but also communicates its context distribution to the agents. As a result, these agents can use this information to determine the ideal trade-off between communication and regret. We prove that under mild assumptions, the environment's context distribution can reduce the required communication bits by a factor proportional to the inverse of the context distribution's sparsity, thereby enabling the agents to achieve near optimal regret with lower communication requirements.

Class imbalance often hinders the effectiveness of machine learning models. Current methods, like undersampling or generating minority samples, aim to mitigate the issue. Our approach, oversampling, may seem counterintuitive, yet it can be an effective technique when done properly. We highlight its benefits and demonstrate its potential to outperform other methods. We further expand its application by proposing an oversampling method for handling multi-label data.

The global heavy-flavour oscillations experiment aims to combine future data from numerous experiments to advance our understanding of heavy-flavour physics. Key research areas include refining measurements of $B^0$ and $D^0$ mixing, investigating rare hadron decays, observing low-helicity suppressed hadron decays, determining the $b\to c\bar{c} d\bar{u}$ amplitude, and analyzing hadron decays involving specific quarks and the Higgs boson. Our research also explores the use of hadron decay amplitudes in constraining the unitary-triangle angle $\gamma$ and studying CP violation in different systems. The GHFEx will have the opportunity to provide insights into multiple particle decays, including some that are rare and some that have not been observed yet.

A significant amount of research time and resources is spent collecting and verifying the validity of experimental results. Replicating studies to verify results is a common practice in many scientific and industrial applications. Due to the complexity of large datasets, machine learning and machine learning assisted reasoning tools are increasingly used to assist in scientific discovery and data analysis. This study explores the use of various machine learning methods for predicting the reproducibility of research findings based on existing bibliometric data. By analyzing the characteristics of 50,000 papers from the NeurIPS collection, we identified key attributes that can help distinguish between correct and false findings. Our results indicate that several simple metrics, such as the number of citations and supporting references, are effective in distinguishing between their accuracy. Moreover, these metrics also contribute to the overall reproducibility of research research.

A groundbreaking technique known as 'flying focus X' has significantly improved the performance of laser-based systems by allowing the focal point to move rapidly through space. This innovation has far-reaching applications in fields such as telecommunications and high-speed sensing technology. The paper presents a new technique that integrates spatial and temporal phase modulation to control the focal point's trajectory. The approach eliminates the need for mechanical focusing lenses in laser systems, reducing their power consumption by nearly eight times. The novel method also offers the capability to move the focal point at high speeds, reaching distances of at least 1 meter per millisecond, while minimizing signal loss. The system's adaptability is further enhanced by its ability to adjust its operating distance in real-time, a feature that is difficult to achieve with conventional phase modulation techniques.

The 2017 FIRA HuroCup Olympic-style competition featured a three-stage tournament featuring 24 robots from around the world. Over seven years, this humanoid robot league has been established with a goal of mimicking a real Olympic event. In the 2017 tournament's first stage, a series of tasks inspired by the Seated Shot Put event were performed, while a defense round allowed the top two performers to be determined. The tournament's final round saw the top two performers compete against each other in a best-of-two-match competition. The success of the HuroCup, which combines the Olympic spirit of competition with robotics advancements, lies in its ability to drive progress in fields such as robotics control, reinforcement learning, and sensor technology.

To enhance cross-domain recommendation, we introduce a new method that aligns two knowledge graphs using metric learning. Our approach formalizes the alignment problem as a classification task in the space of knowledge graphs, and we achieve this by training a network to predict whether two graphs are similar or dissimilar. The resulting network can then be used to compute a similarity matrix representing cross-domain recommendations. Our method outperforms current best practices in a standard benchmark, and we find that incorporating metric learning boosts performance compared to using traditional similarity measures. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a series of ablation experiments.

This research introduces an extended model of automata where finite-state machines can exchange information through a complex network or social structure. The proposed model, denoted as ${\cal N}WFA_{N}$, incorporates network capabilities into weighted finite-state automata. The study examines $N$ weighted finite-state machines that can interact with one another either one-on-one or in groups, and they all produce an output collectively. The main theorem of this paper demonstrates that the expressive power of ${\cal N}WFA_{N}$ is equivalent to that of generalized weighted automata. Furthermore, it is shown that the space complexity of deciding the membership of strings in ${\cal N}WFA_{N}$ is significantly lower than that of ${\cal N}WFA_{MC}$ and also lower than that of generalized weighted automata. The study also investigates the complexity of other operations involving ${\cal N}WFA_{N}$ and draws connections with existing models of automata.

A new model has been proposed to describe heat transfer within two-dimensional (2D) complex plasma layers using a vibrational approach. In this model, the most probable vibrational frequencies, determined by the interaction potential between the plasma particles, are considered, along with the mean effects of an electric field. The resulting energy exchange rate is then calculated by accounting for the mean electric field within the plasma layer. The model takes into account the variation in plasma particle number density, leading to a detailed understanding of the relationship between the vibrational temperature and the plasma temperature in a 2D complex plasma, particularly in the limit of a very small electric field. The model has been applied to the conditions of the Solar Wire (SW) phenomenon, which involves a 2D plasma layer, characterized by a very small electric field and a significant temperature difference between the two ends. The analysis of the Solar Wire data reveals that the vibrational model is consistent with the observed heat transfer in the central section of the plasma layer, provided that the plasma is weakly coupled. Conversely, when the coupling is strong, the model is found to overestimate the energy exchange rate.

This paper explores the connection between infinite-state systems represented by
counter machines with unordered data and coloured Petri nets, showing that this
system of counter machines is equivalent in expressiveness to a more restricted
form of Petri nets with counter, choice, and intersection capabilities. A
direct, practical guide to converting counter machines into Petri nets is presented,
utilizing a data translation process, thereby establishing a link between
finite state machine models and those using counter and intersection capabilities.

To create high frame rate (HFR) videos for coronary angiography, we've developed a new model called the dynamic sparse coding network (DSCN). This model can directly predict coronary angiography videos at HFR using a single low-quality video and corresponding low-frame-rate images. Our proposed model uses a dynamic sparse coding network that produces high-frame-rate videos with superior signal-to-noise ratios compared to existing methods. We tested the DSCN on the HFR coronary angiography dataset provided by the National Medical Systems and Equipment Corporation and achieved significant improvements over the state-of-the-art deep HFR video interpolation methods. Our results on this dataset demonstrate the potential of DSCN in enhancing HFR coronary angiography video quality.

The ultra-low radiation background at the Future Circular Collider's electron-positron collider (FCC-ee) enables researchers to study extremely rare particle decay processes that are currently beyond the reach of other experiments. A new generation of rare particle decay experiments will significantly contribute to our understanding of fundamental symmetries, including precision tests of the Standard Model and searches for new physics. To investigate the potential contributions of FCC-ee to rare particle decay experiments, we examine the feasibility of detecting a hypothetical W boson decay into a muon and neutrino/anti-neutrino. To accurately simulate the FCC-ee experiment, we use a detector model that combines a general-purpose calorimeter with a magnetic muon spectrometer. To optimize the detection process, we utilize a multivariate classifier that incorporates both kinematic and topological properties. Furthermore, we develop a specialized reconstruction algorithm that enables the detection of low-momentum muons in the FCC-ee environment. To estimate the detection efficiency, we utilize the FCC-ee's 5σ dataset, which yields a statistical significance of 1.5σ for the Wμν process at a specific mass level. To further refine the search, we incorporate a Bayesian approach to constrain the mass level of the hypothetical particle, yielding a 95% confidence interval of 2.1-3.1 GeV/c^2. Neutrinos, as non-emitting particles, are abundant within the universe and are known to interact with nuclei through elastic means. Recent findings suggest that using a nucleus as a target in neutrino-nucleus scattering could significantly boost the sensitivity of dark matter experiments due to its potential to detect unobserved dark matter particles. We have conducted a theoretical analysis of how these neutrino interactions impact direct dark matter searches, focusing on a specific scenario where dark matter is driven by its interactions with the galaxy's hot gas. Our results show that the influence of these neutrino interactions on dark matter searches can be substantial, particularly at low levels of dark matter density. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the proposed Geant4 simulation may not be accurate in this regard. We have also explored the potential for future neutrino experiments to detect dark matter, specifically through their ability to determine the galaxy's hot gas density distribution. Our results show that the proposed JUNO and DUNE experiments may be capable of determining this distribution with a precision of 10%, based on their expected sensitivity.

The gravitational influence of a massive black hole on a companion star and its orbit around the black hole can cause star orbits to become irregularly shaped. We investigated how this effect impacts the outcome of a star merger that produces a neutron star or black hole. We used computer simulations to model the merger process of a star and an artificial particle in a rotating frame of reference, taking into account the star's internal structure and the gravitational influence of the black hole. We found that the star's irregularly shaped orbit and rotation result in an uneven distribution of mass within the star, which affects its merger rate and outcome. Specifically, in some scenarios, the star produces a more massive neutron star or black hole than it would without the gravitational influence, potentially altering the properties of compact objects that form through close binary star mergers.

This work investigates solutions to SDEs that are perturbed by fractional Brownian motion with a given Hurst parameter $H$, which is greater than 1/4. We establish SDEs for these solutions and show that they can be solved using Feller-type equations. Our work also derives the key characteristics of solutions in various scenarios, particularly for H less than 1/4. We extend existing results in the field and provide a comprehensive comparison of solution types based on the Hurst parameter $H$. This research is organized into three sections, each focusing on a distinct category of solutions: those defined on a bounded set, those defined on unbounded sets, and those that exist globally. Our work demonstrates how the Hurst parameter $H$ affects solution types and highlights the significance of $H$ in determining solution existence and uniqueness. This research is significant for its exploration of solution uniqueness, which has been a gap in existing literature.

We investigate the concept of nonstationary ideals on ω1, specifically those that can be represented by Σ1 formulas taking set parameters, and find that this is indeed a viable scenario, as previously demonstrated by Bays and Heitmann for the case of formulas without parameters. Furthermore, our work establishes that certain closed unbounded sets defined by nonstationary Σ1 formulas with set parameters have a unique canonical representation. We also show that any nonstationary ideal solely determined by a set parameter has a particular closed unbounded subset, characterized by a formula with a set parameter, such that this subset is in turn characterized by a formula with a set parameter.

The effectiveness of multitask training in enhancing the performance of models on individual tasks has been well-documented. However, the current experimentation methods and the way tasks are selected and grouped together for training lack a comprehensive understanding. Consequently, the true potential of multitask training cannot be fully realized. This paper proposes an approach to improve multitask training through more informed task selection and grouping. By leveraging automated task clustering methods, the proposed approach aims to create more coherent task groups based on their input and output patterns. This is achieved through a novel task embedding space that allows for the identification of subdomains within the overall task space. Empirical evaluations on the GLUE benchmark confirm that the proposed multitask training scheme enhances the performance of standard single-task BERT models, particularly on tasks that benefit from being trained together.

The development of large-scale datasets has significantly enhanced the efficacy of deep learning algorithms for traffic sign recognition, enabling the implementation of transfer learning to facilitate the rapid development of novel detection methods. The creation of a new dataset, MobGTS, was motivated by the need to evaluate the performance of deep learning algorithms across diverse traffic signs, environments, and lighting conditions. MobGTS, a comprehensive dataset, encompasses 9 categories of traffic signs, was captured using a smartphone, and features 24,000 images with detailed annotations, including 7,000 images containing traffic signs. We present an in-depth analysis of the performance of the Fast R-CNN algorithm, a widely employed detection method, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset for the development of innovative algorithms tailored to the specific requirements of the MobGTS.

Recommender systems have become crucial components of our daily lives. The advancements in deep learning have greatly improved their performance. However, traditional methods of training these systems are time-consuming due to the need to collect large amounts of labeled data. The use of these methods often results in a lengthy training time, making it difficult to keep up with the rapidly changing user preferences. To address this issue, we have developed a new framework called SelfCF, which utilizes self-supervised learning and a contrastive loss function to improve model accuracy while significantly reducing training time. The SelfCF framework achieves this by generating pseudo labels for users and items using an autoencoder, and then utilizing these labels to fine-tune its affinity matrix. We have also introduced a new loss function to further enhance the model's performance. The evaluation results of our SelfCF framework, which was tested on multiple benchmark datasets, show a notable improvement in recommendation accuracy, with a significant reduction in training time compared to traditional methods.

The problem of counting a specific class of ramified covers of a complex threefold, subject to additional complexity conditions, is approached using a modified version of topological perturbation theory, which we call higher-dimensional analogs of perturbation theory. By applying this concept, we are able to calculate the invariant that counts these covers, while disregarding certain ramification characteristics, which reflects the ramification type invariant on the covers' class. Furthermore, through explicit calculation, we find the enumerative invariant of covers of the form (C, Spec k) → (C x Spec k / Spec k), where C is a complex curve and k is the field of rational numbers, for a specific type of ramification condition and a specific curve C, specifically the elliptic curve E_n.

Our investigation into the optical properties of the gapped Dirac semimetal Cd$_3$As$_2$ reveals its unique linear dispersion characteristics. At high energy, we find that the density of states and optical conductivity increase in a predictable manner, consistent with a massless Dirac particle. However, below a critical energy, we observe a significant decrease in the density of states, which we attribute to a reduced effective mass due to the linear dispersion. Notably, the linear dispersion's energy scale is roughly 3.7 meV, a value that our analysis suggests may be influenced by the longitudinal dielectric constant.

We analyze the behavior of a population model governed by a slow-fast differential system with periodic coefficients, and establish a connection between this model and a reduced two-point boundary value problem, with a focus on the effect of parameter perturbations on the critical population mass function. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate the significant impact of the period on the critical function's shape, and show that a small period increase can lead to drastic changes in the function's shape, resulting in distinct optimal harvesting biomass and maximum net revenue.

The future advancement of gravitational wave detectors like Einstein Telescope will allow us to explore how black hole binary mergers' waveforms behave in more detailed ways. This increased precision will enable the study of specific wave patterns that current detectors cannot fully measure. In a study focusing on non-spinning black hole binary mergers, we have used numerical simulations to examine the effects of different wave patterns not currently measurable. Our results indicate that second-order wave patterns will be detectable in advanced detectors, yielding 7% and 16% detection rates for binary black holes with masses ranging from 20 to 500 M$_\odot$. Interestingly, the frequency at which these wave patterns become measurable increases with mass, allowing for the study of a larger population of binary black hole mergers.

A recent study discovered a binary in the open cluster NGC 1624, with a 0.1 M_sun companion, with a 200-day orbit. This binary's properties were found through astrometric observations and spectroscopic measurements of the cluster's stars. The study's data showed that the binary's motion was not consistent with a main-sequence star, with a 0.8 arcsecond displacement in 200 days. This binary's classification as a main-sequence star was ruled out, with a high probability that it is a post-main-sequence star. This is the first post-main-sequence star identified through astrometry in an open cluster, with a high probability of 95%. This binary's properties are similar to other post-main-sequence stars, with a mass of 0.1 M_sun and a radius of 0.1 solar radii, as well as a separation of 0.1 AU. This study's data showed that the binary's orbit is consistent with a main-sequence star with a mass of 0.9 M_sun and a radius of 0.9 solar radii, with a probability of 95%. This study's data also showed that the binary's orbit is consistent with a post-main-sequence star with a mass of 0.1 M_sun and a radius of 0.1 solar radii, with a probability of 95%.
